Colorado Regulators Propose Exclusion Rule for Bettor Harassment and Insider Betting

Published November 16, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Colorado's Division of Gaming is proposing changes to Limited Gaming Rule 29 that would let the state's Limited Gaming Control Commission place people on its involuntary exclusion list for threatening athletes, coaches, team staff, or their families, or for betting in violation of the state's insider-betting law. Division Supervisory Investigator Chris Krieger laid out the proposal at a virtual stakeholder workshop this past Thursday, saying the goal is "a tangible and meaningful impact on this issue."

What the proposed rule would cover

The draft rule targets three categories: harassment or threats directed at athletes, coaches, team staff, or their immediate families; insider betting, which is a class 4 felony in Colorado covering athletes, coaches, referees, or anyone else "in a position of trust"; and game manipulation. The list of people the rule would protect is broad — it extends to sports governing bodies and their employees, team and coaching staff and their immediate families, and any staff member or patron of a licensed gaming or sports betting establishment. Krieger noted the division currently can't require sportsbooks to actually block someone placed on the involuntary exclusion list, though it "strongly recommends" operators do so. The division has also stood up a Google Form for athletes and other sports participants to report harassment directly, which Krieger said is meant to encourage more reporting and give the division a way to investigate and loop in local law enforcement.

Colorado isn't the first state to move on this

Ohio was the first state to let its gaming regulator exclude bettors who threaten people connected to sporting events. Last month, the Ohio Casino Control Commission placed an Ohio man on its Sports Gaming Involuntary Exclusion List after an investigation tied threats against a Major League Baseball manager during last year's World Series to bets placed on that series — the first person listed there for threats of violence. West Virginia and Louisiana have since passed their own bills letting regulators exclude bettors who harass athletes, with potential felony exposure attached, and Massachusetts launched an operator-backed reporting system called "Bet on Respect." Colorado's proposal would put it in that same growing group of states treating athlete harassment tied to betting as a regulatory problem, not just a social-media moderation issue for leagues to handle on their own.

Why it matters for bettors

The proposal is still just that — a proposal. Under Colorado's rulemaking process, the commission can't hold a public hearing until at least 30 days after the division files a formal rulemaking notice, and any adopted changes would take roughly 45 to 60 days after a commission vote to actually take effect. For bettors, the relevant takeaway is less about any single state's timeline and more about the direction every one of these rules points: regulators are increasingly willing to treat threats against athletes as something that can cost a bettor their account, not just their standing with a league or platform. Combined with the insider-betting provision, it's also a reminder that "a position of trust" in Colorado's statute reaches further than most bettors probably assume — well past just the athletes themselves.
